**No. Writing all the lyrics does not automatically give you commercial rights to any free AI-generated song.** Your lyrics are one part of the finished work; the generated music, vocals and recording introduce separate rights and contractual questions.

Assuming your lyrics are original and you have not assigned their rights elsewhere, your authorship supports your rights in that text. It does not, by itself, establish ownership of the generated melody, arrangement, synthetic vocal performance or sound recording. Nor does submitting lyrics to a generator establish what permissions the provider gives you for its output.

The useful comparison is:

| Question | What your lyric authorship establishes |
|---|---|
| Can you authorise use of your original lyrics? | Generally yes, subject to any prior agreements or other rights involved. |
| Can you access a free generator or download its output? | Nothing about access or download eligibility; those depend on the service. |
| Can you commercially exploit the complete generated song? | Not automatically; the applicable output licence and account terms must support that use. |
| Can you claim exclusive copyright over every generated element? | Not automatically; copyright protection depends on jurisdiction and the human contribution. |

“Free” describes a price, not a universal licence. A free service might permit commercial use, restrict outputs to personal or noncommercial use, or impose conditions such as attribution. Download access and commercial permission are also separate: being able to obtain an audio file does not establish permission to sell it, monetise it, distribute it commercially or use it in an advertisement.

Commercial permission is distinct from copyright ownership, too. A provider may grant permission to use an output without promising that you own exclusive copyright in all its generated elements. Conversely, uncertainty about copyright protection does not itself supply permission under an applicable service agreement. Commercial use may also require checking third-party material or voice rights if those are involved. Your ownership of the lyrics does not resolve those questions.

Because **no account terms or output licence has been supplied**, the correct conclusion for a particular song is **commercial permission unverified**. That is not a finding that every free AI song is prohibited commercially. It means there is insufficient evidence to say this one is permitted.

To establish permission for a specific output, the relevant evidence would include the service and account tier, the terms applicable when it was generated, the licence covering that output, and any conditions attached to the intended use. A later subscription upgrade should not be assumed to grant rights retroactively unless the terms expressly provide for it. Likewise, an unmonetised promotional video can still involve commercial use.

Under the router’s music guidance, technical availability, approved export, accepted quality and intended-use permission remain independent decisions. Here, only the supplied claim of lyric authorship is available; the account and output permissions remain unknown. No generation, account access, licence verification or publication was performed.

You can therefore retain rights in your original lyrics while still lacking established permission to commercially exploit the complete AI-generated recording. **Lyric ownership clears one rights layer; it does not clear the whole song.**
